'''''Pinus thunbergii''''' ([[synonym (taxonomy)|syn.]] ''Pinus thunbergiana''), the '''Japanese black pine''',<ref name="iucn status 12 November 2021"/><ref name="GDB">{{Cite web |url=https://www.conifers.org/pi/Pinus_thunbergii.php |title=''Pinus thunbergii'' (クロマツ, Japanese black pine) description |website=www.conifers.org |access-date=2019-07-20 |archive-date=2026-01-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260111130616/https://www.conifers.org/pi/Pinus_thunbergii.php |url-status=live }}</ref> is a [[pine]] tree native to coastal areas of Japan ([[Kyūshū]], [[Shikoku]] and [[Honshū]]) and South Korea.<ref name="FoC">{{eFloras |2 |200005368 |Pinus thunbergii |family=Pinaceae |first1=Liguo |last1=Fu |first2=Nan |last2=Li |first3=Thomas S. |last3=Elias |first4=Robert R. |last4=Mill |access-date=2026-08-16 }}</ref>

It is called {{transliteration|ja|kuromatsu}} ({{lang|ja|黒松}}) in [[Japanese language|Japanese]], {{transliteration|ko|gomsol}} ({{lang|ko|곰솔}}) in [[Korean language|Korean]], and {{transliteration|zh|ISO|hēisōng}} ({{lang|zh|黑松}}) in [[Standard Chinese|Chinese]].

== Description ==
[[File:Branches of Pinus thunbergii.jpg|thumb|left|Foliage and cones, Chungcheongnam-do, South Korea]]
Japanese black pines can reach the height of {{Convert|40|m|abbr=off}}, but rarely achieves this size outside its natural range. The [[Bark (botany)|bark]] is grey-brown on young trees and small branches, changing to dark blackish-grey and plated on larger branches and the trunk; becoming quite thick on older trunks. The needles are in [[Fascicle (botany)|fascicles]] of two with a greyish-white sheath at the base, {{Convert|6–12|cm|abbr=off|frac=4}} long. The female (seed) cones are green to purple when immature, ripening pale buff-brown to greyish-buff, {{cvt|4–7|cm|frac=4}} in length, with numerous scales, with small mucro on the tips of the scales, taking a little under two years to maturity and opening in late winter. The male (pollen) cones are {{cvt|1–2|cm|frac=4}} long, borne in clumps of 12–20 at the base of the new spring growth.<ref name="GDB"/><ref name="FoC"/>

== Ecology ==
It occasionally [[hybrid (biology)|hybridises]] with the related ''[[Pinus densiflora]]'' (Japanese red pine); the hybrid has been named ''Pinus × densithunbergii'' by the Japanese botanist Homiki Uyeki.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Pinus × densithunbergii'' Uyeki |website=Plants of the World Online |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:677026-1 |access-date=2026-08-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Uyeki, Homiki |website=International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/a/11012-1 |access-date=2026-08-15}}</ref>

In North America this tree is subject to widespread mortality by the native American pinewood nematode, ''[[Bursaphelenchus xylophilus]]'', spread by means of beetle vectors. Subsequently, [[Blue stain fungi|blue stain fungus]] invades the plant, leading to a rapid decline and death. This [[nematode]] has also been introduced to Japan accidentally, leading to the species becoming endangered in its native area.<ref name="GDB"/>

== Uses ==
In Japan it is widely used as a garden tree, both untrained growing as an overstorey tree, and trained as ''[[niwaki]]''. The trunks and branches are trained from a young age to be elegant and interesting to view. It is one of the classic [[bonsai]] subjects, requiring great patience over many years to train properly.{{citation needed|date=March 2023}}

===Cultivation===
Because of its resistance to pollution and salt, it is a popular horticultural tree. It is a widely adapted plant with attractive dark green foliage.<ref>{{Cite web |title=SelecTree: A Tree Selection Guide |url=https://selectree.calpoly.edu/tree-detail/1081 |access-date=2021-09-22 |website=selectree.calpoly.edu |archive-date=2023-08-12 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230812070144/https://selectree.calpoly.edu/tree-detail/1081 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Second flush of growth ===
One characteristic of the Japanese black pine that makes it desirable for bonsai, is the possibility of inducing a second flush of new growth and improved ramification in a single growing season. The Japanese black pine can be induced to produce new [[bud]]s at the base of each spring candle by cutting the candles near the base as they elongate, a technique called "decandling". This technique will result, in a few weeks, in the flush of multiple new buds where the candle was cut; each of these new buds will result in turn in new candles and branches.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://bonsaitonight.com/2016/07/22/decandling-black-pine-bonsai-overview/ |title=Decandling black pine bonsai - an in-depth guide - Bonsai Tonight |date=22 July 2016 |access-date=20 May 2022 |archive-date=4 May 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220504130412/https://bonsaitonight.com/2016/07/22/decandling-black-pine-bonsai-overview/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
